newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to declare war on crime to save reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to declare war on crime to save reforms.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, in a state of the nation address to parliament on Thursday, will launch a crusade against corruption which is choking Russia's reforms.
Later in the day, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is expected to announce a government shake-up.
Kremlin sources say Yeltsin's chief-of-staff, the liberal Anatoly Chubais, may be taken on as Chernomyrdin's first deputy premier to spearhead the crackdown on economic crime.
"Russia entered 1997 with a heavy load of problems," Yeltsin wrote in his annual address, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.
"More than half its citizens are suffering from delays in wage and pension payments.
"The stranglehold of non-payment is paralysing the economy and the state apparatus is being corroded by corruption," he said. "The authorities barely manage to put laws and decrees into effect."
Yeltsin's speech in the Kremlin's Marble Hall at 11 a.m. (0800 GMT) will last half an hour, official sources said.

It will be a big test of the 66-year-old leader's health after he spent the first eight months of his second term out of action, first due to heart problems and bypass surgery in November and then because of pneumonia.
Yeltsin chided Chernomyrdin last week for the government's poor performance and urged him to put things right immediately.

In his address, the president made clear that first and foremost he wanted the premier to restore order to the country. Otherwise organised crime and corruption threatened to choke the life out of his post-Soviet democratic market reforms.
"An effective market economy is not just freedom for private enterprise but also a strict legal order -- common, stable and generally observed rules of economic activity," Yeltsin said.
"The task of the state is to set such rules and to make sure they are obeyed."

"The problem of economic crime and corruption have grown from what was clearly a police matter into a political issue. The criminal world has in fact openly challenged the state and launched into an open competition with it," he said.
"When free buying and selling extends to the passing of laws, to the work of civil servants and to court decisions, it is not just immoral but a mortal danger to society and the state."
The text, in contrast to last year's was short on concrete economic proposals. Some analysts suggest Yeltsin wants to give Chubais, 41, a free hand to deal with the economy.

Chubais, an outstanding administrator, is popular with foreign investors but hated by the communists who dominate parliament and who accuse him of corruption in his management of Russia's privatisation drive.
Chernomyrdin will chair a government meeting on Thursday afternoon at which he is expected to announce his reshuffle.
Presidential aides and government officials have said that changes in the government will be serious rather than cosmetic.

Some say they expect Chubais to be named first deputy prime minister, with the three cabinet members who currently hold that rank being removed or demoted to leave the Kremlin chief-of-staff as Chernomyrdin's unchallenged number two.

Officials have declined comment on speculation that several key ministers, mainly dealing with finance and social problems, will be axed. Some officials say the changes, should they take place, may be implemented only over time.
